extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for understanding, writing, and criticizing the novel as a literary form (lectures on the components and techniques of the novel: story, people/characters, plot, fantasy, prophecy, pattern and rhythm, point of view, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel definition (extent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel is 'a fiction in prose of a certain extent' — for the purposes of these lectures Forster adds that 'the extent should not be less than 50,000 words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any fictitious prose work over 50,000 words will be treated as a novel for analysis; if a work under that length is to be excluded, reasons should be given. This is a pragmatic working definition, not metaphysical; Forster invites alternative definitions only with persuasive reasons or inclusive adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: English = written in English (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing 'English' literature Forster interprets it as 'written in English,' not geographically limited to England or the British Isles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism limited to 'English' should include works written in English worldwide; geographic publication location or nationality should not unduly constrain the field under discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid period/chronological determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should avoid treating the novel primarily as a product of historical 'periods' and influences; instead visualize novelists as contemporaries, writing from the same inward creative condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: classifying novels by strict period labels ('the novel of the reign of Queen Anne', 'the novel after 1847') or over-emphasizing influence and school. Prefer close attention to what the novel itself does rather than which decade it belongs to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read books thoroughly (no armchair classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books 'have to be read' — classification and criticism based on second-hand facts, dates, or categories is pseudo-scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the habit of relating a book to external facts (dates, author's biography, tendencies) before understanding its content. The critic must sit down and struggle with the book itself; otherwise classifications (by date, subject, or 'tendency') are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware pseudo‑scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudo‑scholars imitate scholarly forms (classification, mention of 'genius', lists of tones) without the reading or understanding to back them up; such methods are misleading for critical judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include exhaustive taxonomies (by weather, tone, locality, sex, point of view) offered as though exhaustive, the constant appeal to 'genius' as a substitute for analysis, and using 'tendency' as a portable critical tag. Critics should resist these shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novel's value: sensitiveness over subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's success lies in its 'sensitiveness' — the author's acuity of perception and handling — rather than in the inherent importance of its subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that topicality (e.g., writing about a political movement or historical event) makes a novel great. Evaluate how sensitively the novelist handles human experience and material, not merely whether the subject seems significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs Plot (structural distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster's functional distinction: a 'story' is a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence; a 'plot' arranges events to show causal relationships (events connected by cause and effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating structure, ask whether the sequence is presented for chronological interest (story) or structured to emphasize causation and complication (plot). Both are legitimate but different aims and produce different reader effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters: flat (one‑idea) vs round (complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are built around a single idea or trait and can be summarized simply; round characters are complex, capable of surprising the reader in ways that remain believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'flat' characters where a consistent, reliable figure is needed (comic devices, allegory); aim for 'round' characters when the novelist's goal is psychological truth and surprise. A test: can the character surprise you convincingly?

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view and technique of conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques like choice of narrator, use of 'he said'/'she said' tags, and the handling of interiority vary across time and alter the tone and effect of dialogue and representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the appropriateness of point of view to the novel's aims (omniscient, limited, first person, free indirect discourse). Notice how reporting speech (dialogue punctuation, speech tags) affects the reader's perception of characters and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (mode and execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy in fiction operates by starting with a small object or detail, 'taking a flutter from it' and returning to it; combines humorous sense of life's muddle with an appreciation of beauty. Execution differentiates writers within the same tradition (e.g., Sterne vs Woolf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fantasy by how it manipulates attention to small objects/events, by tone (deliberate bewilderment, sentimentalism vs aloofness), and by technique: are the odd effects coherent and artistically justified?

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy (novelistic function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster treats 'prophecy' as an aspect to be defined and explored (chapter on 'Prophecy'); prophecy in the novel is not the same as prediction but a way of conveying larger truth or a sense of human destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering prophetic elements, assess whether anticipatory or visionary passages expand the novel's sense of meaning without reducing characters to mouthpieces or forcing didactic conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern (recurrence and symbolic structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern in fiction is an arrangement of motifs, images, or themes that recurs across a work; it can act as a 'binding' device but must not harden into mere symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repetition combined with variation (see rhythm). Patterns should assist unity and create resonances; beware of patterns used mechanically (e.g., recurring object-as-banner) that only draw attention to themselves without enriching meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm defined (repetition plus variation; two kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy rhythm: tactile, repetitive motifs (the 'diddidy dum') that readers can 'tap' to; complex rhythm: larger-scale relations across the whole work (analogy to a symphony) harder to detect. Rhythm in fiction may be 'repetition plus variation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good rhythmic devices (e.g., Proust’s 'little phrase') recur with variation to stitch the book internally. Rhythm should wax and wane to surprise and refresh; when done badly it becomes boring and symbolic. Rhythm often arises organically rather than via preplanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leitmotif/'little phrase' as internal stitching
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring musical or thematic phrase (Forster's example: Vinteuil's 'little phrase' in Proust) can function like an internally mobile element that reappears in different contexts and binds disparate parts of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether recurring motifs change shape and resonance over time, contributing to unity without degenerating into mere banners. Effective motifs may be forgotten and later return altered, creating orienting moments for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion (novelistic ambition vs completion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's ideal tendency is toward 'expansion' — opening out and liberating its elements — rather than neat 'completion' or rounding off. Forster analogizes this to the symphony whose parts, when liberated, form a larger whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a novel achieves a sense of enlargement (themes and characters taking on greater life) rather than forcing closure. Untidiness can be productive if it yields larger chords and resonances behind the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique can change across generations (tradition matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even while basic human concerns remain constant, literary technique (uses of conversation, fantasy methods, humouring devices) shifts across time and constitutes 'literary tradition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a novel, distinguish between enduring human elements and historically determined techniques; study how an author inherits and modifies traditions and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist's primary problem: human beings
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama may accommodate pictorial or formal constraints, but the novel is deeply committed to representing human beings; the novelist must give his characters a 'good run' while achieving an aesthetic beyond mere reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how fully characters are rendered as living beings; the novelist should balance attention to human complexity with broader artistic aims (pattern, rhythm, theme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: personal vs impersonal (and need for talent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone may be personal or impersonal, but Forster warns the pseudo‑scholar that simply classifying tone is insufficient without recognizing the role of the author's talent/genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When noting tone, consider how tone was achieved (technique, voice, perspective); do not treat tone labelling as explanatory in itself—investigate the means of its production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincialism is a fault in criticism (not necessarily in fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provincialism may be a source of strength in writers but is a serious fault in critics, who must cultivate a wide outlook and avoid narrowness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid parochial standards when judging novels and should be willing to place local masterpieces beside canonical world literature to see their true scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing criticism to external facts (tendency/eclecticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relating a book primarily to external facts (author biography, social tendencies, historical events) is an inadequate method of criticism; such 'tendency' arguments are transportable but often shallow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contextual facts to inform judgment but not to substitute for close reading. The critic's first obligation is to the text and to understanding how it produces meaning and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration and the creative state (critical focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster emphasizes a shared creative condition ('inspiration') across writers of different ages; critics should attend to this inward process rather than only to outward historical differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing authors, consider evidence of a similar imaginative state that transcends chronology; this supports comparative approaches that focus on technique and sensibility rather than mere date.
